# Reference Card

Graded output is what exists on disk at the
end of the run. Reasoning without file changes
does not count.

## Turn sequence

1. Identify the deliverable: path, name, format,
   and required behavior.
2. Read the task instruction and every source file
   it references. Do not guess from names or categories.
3. Write a structurally valid stub to the output path
   immediately. Update that file in place afterward.
4. Before touching a resource that may change on access,
   copy it to a working location and use the copy.
5. Save a working attempt once it is plausible.
6. Validate with checks you control: compile, run,
   read back, or probe behavior. Read failures literally.
7. Fix the named issue, save, and re-validate.
8. After three failures with the same structure, change
   the approach — not just the parameters.

One short plan, then act.

## Hard constraints

Output location, naming, and format are fixed requirements.
Meet them exactly before optimizing content quality.

Literal values in the task — paths, names, dates, field
labels, separators — are part of the contract. Reproduce
them exactly. When sample output is provided, match its
format character for character.

## Read before you write

When output must interact with an existing component,
read its implementation first. Documentation states
intent; code defines behavior.

When data passes through multiple steps, inspect what
each step actually produces before assuming what the
next step will see.

## Preserve before you probe

Stateful resources may change when opened or executed.
Copy to a working location first when the original state
must remain unchanged.

## Root-cause discipline

When something fails, use the error message to locate
the failing check in source or configuration. Apply the
smallest change that addresses that check. Re-validate
after each change.

When the deliverable is a patch or diff, generate it
with version-control tooling when available, verify it
applies cleanly on a copy of the tree, and write it to
the path named in the task.

## Values from the workspace

Required values must come from reading the actual sources
in the workspace. Search broadly — paths, extensions, and
representations — before concluding a value is absent.

## Verify effects, not intentions

An action counts only after you confirm the effect:
file written → read it back; command run → inspect output;
configuration changed → confirm the running behavior you
care about.

## Tools

Use whatever tools are already available in the environment:
shell, interpreters, file I/O, debuggers, and standard
utilities. Prefer installed packages and the standard library;
avoid importing packages that are not present.

## Code hygiene

Smallest patch that fixes the failure. Stable clocks for
timing. Validate at trust boundaries. Comments only for
non-obvious reasoning.

When content includes shell-special characters, write
files with direct file tools, then read back to confirm.

## Stop condition

Re-read the output artifact. If it does not match your
current understanding, update it. What is on disk when
you stop is the deliverable.
